variable {α : Type u} {H : Hilbert α}
informal_statement: Hilbert's KC axiom is weaker than Hilbert's LC axiom.
informal_proof: Within Hilbert's logical system, we consider the relationship between the KC and LC axioms. The KC axiom is shown to be weaker by demonstrating that, when combined with the law of excluded middle (PEM), it implies the LC axiom. This implies that any proof derived using KC can also be derived using LC, given the inclusion of PEM. Thus, the KC axiom does not independently prove LC, establishing its weaker position relative to LC.

import Foundation.Logic.HilbertStyle.Supplemental
import Foundation.IntProp.Formula

namespace LO.IntProp

variable {α : Type u}

structure Hilbert (α) where
  axioms : Theory α

namespace Hilbert

variable {H : Hilbert α}


section

class IncludeEFQ (H : Hilbert α) where
  include_EFQ : 𝗘𝗙𝗤 ⊆ H.axioms := by simp

class IncludeLEM (H : Hilbert α) where

class IncludeDNE (H : Hilbert α) where

end

  | and₁ φ ψ     : Deduction H $ φ ⋏ ψ ➝ φ
  | and₂ φ ψ     : Deduction H $ φ ⋏ ψ ➝ ψ
  | and₃ φ ψ     : Deduction H $ φ ➝ ψ ➝ φ ⋏ ψ

  | neg_equiv φ  : Deduction H $ Axioms.NegEquiv φ

variable {α : Type u} {H : Hilbert α}
informal_statement: Hilbert's consistency condition (LC) is a logical condition that is weaker than Hilbert's completeness condition (Cl). This means that if a system satisfies Cl, it automatically satisfies LC, but not necessarily the other way around.
informal_proof:
To establish that Hilbert's consistency condition (LC) is weaker than Hilbert's completeness condition (Cl), we need to demonstrate that any system that satisfies Cl also satisfies LC. 

First, consider a system that meets the requirements of Cl. Within this system, we can apply the established theorem that connects the subset relations of conditions to their logical strength. This involves considering whether a condition implies another in the context of the system's axioms and rules.

By analyzing the structure of the conditions and applying the simplifications enabled by known lemmas (such as ex falso quodlibet and Dummett's axiom), we can systematically show that the satisfaction of Cl leads inevitably to the satisfaction of LC. This process involves breaking down the implications of Cl and demonstrating that they also satisfy the less stringent requirements of LC.

Thus, through careful logical analysis and application of foundational theorems, we confirm that Hilbert's consistency condition (LC) is indeed weaker than Hilbert's completeness condition (Cl).

import Foundation.Logic.HilbertStyle.Basic
import Foundation.Logic.HilbertStyle.Supplemental
import Foundation.IntProp.Formula

namespace LO.IntProp

variable {α : Type u}

structure Hilbert (α) where
  axioms : Theory α

namespace Hilbert

variable {H : Hilbert α}


section

class IncludeEFQ (H : Hilbert α) where
  include_EFQ : 𝗘𝗙𝗤 ⊆ H.axioms := by simp

class IncludeLEM (H : Hilbert α) where
  include_LEM : 𝗟𝗘𝗠 ⊆ H.axioms := by simp

class IncludeDNE (H : Hilbert α) where
  include_DNE : 𝗗𝗡𝗘 ⊆ H.axioms := by simp

end


inductive Deduction (H : Hilbert α) : Formula α → Type _
  | eaxm {φ}     : φ ∈ H.axioms → Deduction H φ
  | mdp {φ ψ}    : Deduction H (φ ➝ ψ) → Deduction H φ → Deduction H ψ
  | verum        : Deduction H $ ⊤
  | imply₁ φ ψ   : Deduction H $ φ ➝ ψ ➝ φ
  | imply₂ φ ψ χ : Deduction H $ (φ ➝ ψ ➝ χ) ➝ (φ ➝ ψ) ➝ φ ➝ χ
  | and₁ φ ψ     : Deduction H $ φ ⋏ ψ ➝ φ
  | and₂ φ ψ     : Deduction H $ φ ⋏ ψ ➝ ψ
  | and₃ φ ψ     : Deduction H $ φ ➝ ψ ➝ φ ⋏ ψ
  | or₁ φ ψ      : Deduction H $ φ ➝ φ ⋎ ψ
  | or₂ φ ψ      : Deduction H $ ψ ➝ φ ⋎ ψ
  | or₃ φ ψ χ    : Deduction H $ (φ ➝ χ) ➝ (ψ ➝ χ) ➝ (φ ⋎ ψ ➝ χ)
  | neg_equiv φ  : Deduction H $ Axioms.NegEquiv φ

rag.name: LO.IntProp.Formula.cases'
rag.content:
@[elab_as_elim]
def cases' {C : Formula α → Sort w}
    (hfalsum : C ⊥)
    (hverum  : C ⊤)
    (hatom   : ∀ a : α, C (atom a))
    (hneg    : ∀ φ : Formula α, C (∼φ))
    (himp    : ∀ (φ ψ : Formula α), C (φ ➝ ψ))
    (hand    : ∀ (φ ψ : Formula α), C (φ ⋏ ψ))
    (hor     : ∀ (φ ψ : Formula α), C (φ ⋎ ψ))
    : (φ : Formula α) → C φ
  | ⊥       => hfalsum
  | ⊤       => hverum
  | atom a  => hatom a
  | ∼φ      => hneg φ
  | φ ➝ ψ  => himp φ ψ
  | φ ⋏ ψ   => hand φ ψ
  | φ ⋎ ψ   => hor φ ψ

informal_statement: Hilbert'sKC system is weaker than Hilbert'sCl system.
informal_proof: Hilbert'sKC system is weaker than Hilbert'sCl system because it avoids certain axioms or employs less powerful axioms, making every theorem provable inKC also provable inCl. The systemCl incorporates stronger axioms that compensate for the absence of certain principles inKC, thereby ensuring that all theorems provable inKC are included withinCl, but not necessarily the other way around.

rag.name: Equiv.equiv_subsingleton_dom
rag.content:
instance equiv_subsingleton_dom [Subsingleton α] : Subsingleton (α ≃ β) :=
  ⟨fun f _ => Equiv.ext fun _ => @Subsingleton.elim _ (Equiv.subsingleton.symm f) _ _⟩

rag.name: subset_refl

rag.name: Collection.subset_trans
rag.content:
@[trans] lemma subset_trans {a b c : α} (ha : a ⊆ b) (hb : b ⊆ c) : a ⊆ c :=

informal_statement: If the axioms of Hilbert system \( H₁ \) are a subset of the axioms of Hilbert system \( H₂ \), then \( H₁ \) is weaker than \( H₂ \).
informal_proof: Given two Hilbert systems \( H₁ \) and \( H₂ \), assume that all axioms of \( H₁ \) are included within \( H₂ \). This means that any formula that is derivable in \( H₁ \) is also a formula in \( H₂ \) since all the axioms and rules of inference available in \( H₁ \) are also present in \( H₂ \). Therefore, any proof in \( H₁ \) can also be constructed as a proof in \( H₂ \). Consequently, \( H₂ \) is capable of proving all the theorems that \( H₁ \) can prove, if not more, due to the additional axioms it possesses. This demonstrates that \( H₁ \) is weaker than \( H₂ \) because it cannot prove any theorem that \( H₂ \) cannot prove, while \( H₂ \) is more expressive as it has a broader set of axioms to derive further truths. Hence, \( H₁ \) is weaker than \( H₂ \).

namespace LO.IntProp.Hilbert

variable {α : Type u} {H : Hilbert α}
informal_statement: If every axiom of a Hilbert system H₁ is derivable in another Hilbert system H₂, then H₁ is weaker than H₂.
informal_proof: Assume that H₁ and H₂ are Hilbert systems. If every axiom in H₁ is derivable in H₂, meaning that for each axiom φ in H₁, H₂ can prove φ, then by the definition of a weaker system, H₁ is weaker than H₂. This is because being weaker implies that H₁'s axioms are a subset of H₂'s theorems, making H₁ less comprehensive or powerful compared to H₂.

rag.name: LO.IntProp.Formula.rec'
rag.content:
@[elab_as_elim]
def rec' {C : Formula α → Sort w}
  (hfalsum : C ⊥)
  (hverum  : C ⊤)
  (hatom   : ∀ a : α, C (atom a))
  (hneg    : ∀ φ : Formula α, C φ → C (∼φ))
  (himp    : ∀ (φ ψ : Formula α), C φ → C ψ → C (φ ➝ ψ))
  (hand    : ∀ (φ ψ : Formula α), C φ → C ψ → C (φ ⋏ ψ))
  (hor     : ∀ (φ ψ : Formula α), C φ → C ψ → C (φ ⋎ ψ))
  : (φ : Formula α) → C φ
  | ⊥       => hfalsum
  | ⊤       => hverum
  | atom a  => hatom a
  | ∼φ      => hneg φ (rec' hfalsum hverum hatom hneg himp hand hor φ)
  | φ ➝ ψ  => himp φ ψ (rec' hfalsum hverum hatom hneg himp hand hor φ) (rec' hfalsum hverum hatom hneg himp hand hor ψ)
  | φ ⋏ ψ   => hand φ ψ (rec' hfalsum hverum hatom hneg himp hand hor φ) (rec' hfalsum hverum hatom hneg himp hand hor ψ)
  | φ ⋎ ψ   => hor φ ψ (rec' hfalsum hverum hatom hneg himp hand hor φ) (rec' hfalsum hverum hatom hneg himp hand hor ψ)

rag.content:
@[elab_as_elim]
def cases' {C : Formula α → Sort w}
    (hfalsum : C ⊥)
    (hverum  : C ⊤)
    (hatom   : ∀ a : α, C (atom a))
    (hneg    : ∀ φ : Formula α, C (∼φ))
    (himp    : ∀ (φ ψ : Formula α), C (φ ➝ ψ))
    (hand    : ∀ (φ ψ : Formula α), C (φ ⋏ ψ))
    (hor     : ∀ (φ ψ : Formula α), C (φ ⋎ ψ))
    : (φ : Formula α) → C φ
  | ⊥       => hfalsum
  | ⊤       => hverum
  | atom a  => hatom a
  | ∼φ      => hneg φ
  | φ ➝ ψ  => himp φ ψ
  | φ ⋏ ψ   => hand φ ψ
  | φ ⋎ ψ   => hor φ ψ

variable {α : Type u} {H : Hilbert α}
informal_statement: Given a formula that can be derived in the Hilbert system, this function constructs a proof for it by systematically applying the defined inference rules for all logical connectives, ensuring that every logical step is justified through the appropriate introduction or elimination rules.
informal_proof:
To prove that the function `rec!` constructs a valid proof for any formula derivable in the Hilbert system, we proceed by induction on the structure of the formula, following the defined inference rules.

1. **Base Case**: If the formula is an axiom (`a ∈ H.axioms`), then by definition, `rec!` directly applies the axiom to construct the proof, resulting in a valid derivation.

2. **Inductive Step**: Assume that for all formulas of a certain complexity, `rec!` can construct proofs following the established inference rules. Now, consider a more complex formula:

   - **Implication (`φ → ψ`)**: Using the `imply₁` rule, `rec!` assumes the antecedent `φ` and, based on the induction hypothesis, applies the appropriate rules to derive `ψ`, thereby constructing a proof for `φ → ψ`.

   - **Conjunction (`φ ∧ ψ`)**:The `and₁` and `and₂` rules are applied separately to derive `φ` and `ψ`, respectively, ensuring that both components of the conjunction are proven, thus constructing a proof for `φ ∧ ψ`.

   - **Disjunction (`φ ∨ ψ`)**:Using the `or₁`, `or₂`, and `or₃` rules, `rec!` handles each case individually, constructing proofs for each possible disjunct to establish a valid derivation for `φ ∨ ψ`.

   - **Negation (`¬φ`)**:By employing the `neg_equiv` rule, `rec!` translates the negation into an implication (`φ → ⊥`), and applies the corresponding inference rules to construct a valid proof.

3. **Conclusion**: By systematically applying the inference rules corresponding to each logical connective, `rec!` ensures that every derivable formula in the Hilbert system receives a valid proof, thus establishing the completeness of the proof construction process.

<STATEMENT>

If φ is an axiom in the Hilbert-style calculus H, then H proves φ with uniqueness.

</STATEMENT>

<PROOF>

1. **Understanding the Context**:
   - **H**: A Hilbert-style calculus over an alphabet α.
   - **φ**: A formula in the language defined by α.
   - **H.axioms**: The set of axioms within the system H.

2. **Given**:
   - φ is an axiom in H, i.e., φ ∈ H.axioms.

3. **To Prove**:
   - H proves φ with uniqueness, written as H ⊢! φ.

4. **Proof Steps**:
   - **Step 1**: By the definition of a Hilbert-style calculus, axioms are formulas that are directly provable without any premises. Therefore, if φ is in H.axioms, it is immediately a theorem of H.
   - **Step 2**: Since φ is an axiom, there is a direct, straightforward derivation of φ without the need for additional axioms or rules of inference beyond those already defined in H.
   - **Step 3**: The uniqueness aspect ensures that there is no alternative derivation of φ; hence, the proof is both direct and unique.

5. **Conclusion**:
   - Therefore, if φ is an axiom in H, H ⊢! φ, as φ can be formally derived in one step from the axioms.

rag.name: Finset.exists_minimal
rag.content:
theorem Finset.exists_minimal {α : Type*} [Preorder α] (s : Finset α) (h : s.Nonempty) :
    ∃ m ∈ s, ∀ x ∈ s, ¬x < m := by
  obtain ⟨c, hcs : c ∈ s⟩ := h
  have : WellFounded (@LT.lt { x // x ∈ s } _) := Finite.wellFounded_of_trans_of_irrefl _
  obtain ⟨⟨m, hms : m ∈ s⟩, -, H⟩ := this.has_min Set.univ ⟨⟨c, hcs⟩, trivial⟩
  exact ⟨m, hms, fun x hx hxm => H ⟨x, hx⟩ trivial hxm⟩

rag.name: Finset.exists_sup_ge
rag.content:
theorem exists_sup_ge [SemilatticeSup β] [OrderBot β] [WellFoundedGT β] (f : α → β) :
    ∃ t : Finset α, ∀ a, f a ≤ t.sup f := by
  cases isEmpty_or_nonempty α
  · exact ⟨⊥, isEmptyElim⟩
  obtain ⟨_, ⟨t, rfl⟩, ht⟩ := wellFounded_gt.has_min _ (Set.range_nonempty (sup · f))
  refine ⟨t, fun a ↦ ?_⟩
  classical
  have := ht (f a ⊔ t.sup f) ⟨insert a t, by simp⟩
  rwa [GT.gt, right_lt_sup, not_not] at this

rag.name: Part.le_total_of_le_of_le
rag.content:
theorem le_total_of_le_of_le {x y : Part α} (z : Part α) (hx : x ≤ z) (hy : y ≤ z) :
    x ≤ y ∨ y ≤ x := by
  rcases Part.eq_none_or_eq_some x with (h | ⟨b, h₀⟩)
  · rw [h]
    left
    apply OrderBot.bot_le _
  right; intro b' h₁
  rw [Part.eq_some_iff] at h₀
  have hx := hx _ h₀; have hy := hy _ h₁
  have hx := Part.mem_unique hx hy; subst hx
  exact h₀

rag.name: Lean.Elab.Tactic.closeMainGoal
rag.content:
/--
Closes main goal using the given expression.
If `checkUnassigned == true`, then `val` must not contain unassigned metavariables.
Returns `true` if `val` was successfully used to close the goal.
-/
def closeMainGoal (tacName : Name) (val : Expr) (checkUnassigned := true): TacticM Unit := do
  if checkUnassigned then
    ensureHasNoMVars val
  let mvarId ← getMainGoal
  if (← mvarId.checkedAssign val) then
    replaceMainGoal []
  else
    throwTacticEx tacName mvarId m!"attempting to close the goal using{indentExpr val}\nthis is often due occurs-check failure"

rag.name: Lean.Elab.Tactic.closeUsingOrAdmit
rag.content:
/-- Close the main goal using the given tactic. If it fails, log the error and `admit` -/
def closeUsingOrAdmit (tac : TacticM Unit) : TacticM Unit := do
  /- Important: we must define `closeUsingOrAdmit` before we define
     the instance `MonadExcept` for `TacticM` since it backtracks the state including error messages. -/
  let mvarId :: mvarIds ← getUnsolvedGoals | throwNoGoalsToBeSolved
  tryCatchRuntimeEx
    (focusAndDone tac)
    fun ex => do
      if (← read).recover then
        logException ex
        admitGoal mvarId
        setGoals mvarIds
      else
        throw ex

def cases' {C : Formula α → Sort w}
    (hfalsum : C ⊥)
    (hverum  : C ⊤)
    (hatom   : ∀ a : α, C (atom a))
    (hneg    : ∀ φ : Formula α, C (∼φ))
    (himp    : ∀ (φ ψ : Formula α), C (φ ➝ ψ))
    (hand    : ∀ (φ ψ : Formula α), C (φ ⋏ ψ))
    (hor     : ∀ (φ ψ : Formula α), C (φ ⋎ ψ))
    : (φ : Formula α) → C φ
  | ⊥       => hfalsum
  | ⊤       => hverum
  | atom a  => hatom a
  | ∼φ      => hneg φ
  | φ ➝ ψ  => himp φ ψ
  | φ ⋏ ψ   => hand φ ψ
  | φ ⋎ ψ   => hor φ ψ

\text{mdp}(\text{mdp}(h₁, h₂), h₃) = \text{mdp}(h₁, \text{mdp}(h₂, h₃))
\]

Assuming that `mdp` is a composition operation that is associative by definition or by its underlying properties (such as congruence and associativity as seen in the formal proof), the application of `mdp` in different groupings does not alter the final outcome. Therefore, the equivalence above holds true, confirming that the operation `mdp` is associative.

Hence, we have established that `mdp(mdp(h₁, h₂), h₃)` is indeed equivalent to `mdp(h₁, mdp(h₂, h₃))`, thereby proving the associativity of the `mdp` operation.

variable {α : Type u} {H : Hilbert α}
informal_statement: If φ implies χ and ψ implies χ, then either φ or ψ implies χ.
informal_proof:
We aim to prove that if φ implies χ and ψ implies χ, then the disjunction φ ⋎ ψ also implies χ. 

To do this, we will use a case analysis on the disjunction φ ⋎ ψ:

1. **Case 1:** Assume φ is true.
   - Since φ implies χ (given), χ must be true.
   
2. **Case 2:** Assume ψ is true.
   - Since ψ implies χ (given), χ must be true.

In both cases, χ follows. Therefore, if φ or ψ is true, χ must be true. This completes the proof that (φ ⋎ ψ) implies χ.

informal_statement: For any proposition φ, φ is logically equivalent to its negation.
informal_proof:
To establish that φ is equivalent to its negation, we proceed in two directions.

First, assume φ is true. By the definition of negation, ¬φ (the negation of φ) must be false. Conversely, if ¬φ is true, then φ must be false. This bidirectional implication shows that φ and ¬φ cannot both be true simultaneously, and if one is true, the other must be false, thereby establishing their logical equivalence.

informal_statement: If φ implies that ψ implies χ, then from φ and ψ, we can derive χ.
informal_proof:
1. We start by assuming φ is true.
2. Given the hypothesis that φ and ψ together lead to χ, and since φ is true, we now focus on ψ.
3. Assuming ψ is also true, we can use the given hypothesis that φ together with ψ leads to χ.
4. Therefore, starting from φ and ψ, we can derive χ.

variable {α : Type u} {H : Hilbert α}
informal_statement: A Hilbert-style deduction system for a set of axioms \( H \) allows us to derive logical formulas based on specific rules of inference. Starting from the axioms of \( H \), we can apply these rules to systematically prove the validity of more complex formulas within the system.
informal_proof:
To understand how formulas are derived within this Hilbert-style system, let's examine the rules of inference:

1. **Axioms (\( \varepsilon xm \))**: Any axiom \( \varphi \) in \( H \) is directly deducible, denoted as \( \varphi \in \text{Deduction}_H \).

2. **Modus Ponens (\( mdp \))**: If we can deduce \( \varphi \rightarrow \psi \) and have a deduction of \( \varphi \), then we can conclude \( \psi \).

3. **Tautology (\( verum \))**: The tautology \( \top \) is always deducible, reflecting that certain statements are universally true.

4. **Implication Introduction (\( imply_1 \))**: Allows us to assert that if \( \varphi \) implies \( \psi \rightarrow \varphi \), then it is logically consistent within the system.

5. **Implication Elimination (\( imply_2 \))**: Helps manage more complex implications involving multiple propositions.

6. **Conjunction Introduction and Elimination (\( and_1 \), \( and_2 \), \( and_3 \))**: These rules permit breaking down conjunctions (\( \land \)) into their individual components or reassembling them from implications.

7. **Disjunction Introduction and Elimination (\( or_1 \), \( or_2 \), \( or_3 \))**: These rules address disjunctions (\( \lor \)), allowing for flexible reasoning in either part of a disjunction.

8. **Negation Equivalence (\( neg_equiv \))**: Establishes the relationship between negation and other logical connectives.

By systematically applying these rules starting from the axioms, we can construct proofs for more intricate formulas within the system. Each rule ensures that if the premises (antecedents) are true (derivable), then the conclusion (consequent) must also be true (derivable). Thus, the inductive definition of "Deduction" accurately captures the process of logical derivation within this Hilbert-style framework.

variable {α : Type u} {H : Hilbert α}
informal_statement: For any propositions $a$ and $b$, $a \land b$ is equivalent to $b \land a$.
informal_proof:
We aim to prove that for any propositions $a$ and $b$, the conjunction $a \land b$ is equivalent to $b \land a$. This property, known as commutativity, ensures that the order of propositions in an 'and' statement does not affect its truth value.

Assuming $a \land b$ is true, by the definition of conjunction, both $a$ and $b$ must individually hold true. Since conjunction is commutative, swapping the propositions $a$ and $b$ does not change the truth value of the conjunction. Therefore, $b \land a$ must also be true.

Conversely, if $b \land a$ is true, the same reasoning applies: both $b$ and $a$ are true, and thus $a \land b$ is also true.

Hence, we have shown that $a \land b$ is equivalent to $b \land a$, establishing the commutative property of conjunction in this logical system.

rag.name: Mathlib.Notation3.notation3
rag.content:
/--
`notation3` declares notation using Lean-3-style syntax.

Examples:
```
notation3 "∀ᶠ " (...) " in " f ", " r:(scoped p => Filter.eventually p f) => r
notation3 "MyList[" (x", "* => foldr (a b => MyList.cons a b) MyList.nil) "]" => x
```
By default notation is unable to mention any variables defined using `variable`, but
`local notation3` is able to use such local variables.

Use `notation3 (prettyPrint := false)` to keep the command from generating a pretty printer
for the notation.

This command can be used in mathlib4 but it has an uncertain future and was created primarily
for backward compatibility.
-/
elab (name := notation3) doc:(docComment)? attrs?:(Parser.Term.attributes)? attrKind:Term.attrKind
    "notation3" prec?:(precedence)? name?:(namedName)? prio?:(namedPrio)?
    pp?:(ppSpace prettyPrintOpt)? items:(ppSpace notation3Item)+ " => " val:term : command => do
  -- We use raw `Name`s for variables. This maps variable names back to the
  -- identifiers that appear in `items`
  let mut boundIdents : Std.HashMap Name Ident := {}
  -- Replacements to use for the `macro`
  let mut boundValues : Std.HashMap Name Syntax := {}
  -- The names of the bound names in order, used when constructing patterns for delaboration.
  let mut boundNames : Array Name := #[]
  -- The normal/foldl/foldr type of each variable (for delaborator)
  let mut boundType : Std.HashMap Name BoundValueType := {}
  -- Function to update `syntaxArgs` and `pattArgs` using `macroArg` syntax
  let pushMacro (syntaxArgs : Array (TSyntax `stx)) (pattArgs : Array Syntax)
      (mac : TSyntax ``macroArg) := do
    let (syntaxArg, pattArg) ← expandMacroArg mac
    return (syntaxArgs.push syntaxArg, pattArgs.push pattArg)
  -- Arguments for the `syntax` command
  let mut syntaxArgs := #[]
  -- Arguments for the LHS pattern in the `macro`. Also used to construct the syntax
  -- when delaborating
  let mut pattArgs := #[]
  -- The matchers to assemble into a delaborator
  let mut matchers := #[]
  -- Whether we've seen a `(...)` item
  let mut hasBindersItem := false
  -- Whether we've seen a `scoped` item
  let mut hasScoped := false
  for item in items do
    match item with
    | `(notation3Item| $lit:str) =>
      -- Can't use `pushMacro` since it inserts an extra variable into the pattern for `str`, which
      -- breaks our delaborator
      syntaxArgs := syntaxArgs.push (← `(stx| $lit:str))
      pattArgs := pattArgs.push <| mkAtomFrom lit lit.1.isStrLit?.get!
    | `(notation3Item| $_:bindersItem) =>
      if hasBindersItem then
        throwErrorAt item "Cannot have more than one `(...)` item."
      hasBindersItem := true
      -- HACK: Lean 3 traditionally puts a space after the main binder atom, resulting in
      -- notation3 "∑ "(...)", "r:(scoped f => sum f) => r
      -- but extBinders already has a space before it so we strip the trailing space of "∑ "
      if let `(stx| $lit:str) := syntaxArgs.back! then
        syntaxArgs := syntaxArgs.pop.push (← `(stx| $(quote lit.getString.trimRight):str))
      (syntaxArgs, pattArgs) ← pushMacro syntaxArgs pattArgs (← `(macroArg| binders:extBinders))
    | `(notation3Item| ($id:ident $sep:str* $(prec?)? => $kind ($x $y => $scopedTerm) $init)) =>
      (syntaxArgs, pattArgs) ← pushMacro syntaxArgs pattArgs <| ←
        `(macroArg| $id:ident:sepBy(term $(prec?)?, $sep:str))
      -- N.B. `Syntax.getId` returns `.anonymous` for non-idents
      let scopedTerm' ← scopedTerm.replaceM fun s => pure boundValues[s.getId]?
      let init' ← init.replaceM fun s => pure boundValues[s.getId]?
      boundIdents := boundIdents.insert id.getId id
      match kind with
        | `(foldKind| foldl) =>
          boundValues := boundValues.insert id.getId <| ←
            `(expand_foldl% ($x $y => $scopedTerm') $init' [$$(.ofElems $id),*])
          boundNames := boundNames.push id.getId
          boundType := boundType.insert id.getId .foldl
          matchers := matchers.push <|
            mkFoldlMatcher id.getId x.getId y.getId scopedTerm init boundNames
        | `(foldKind| foldr) =>
          boundValues := boundValues.insert id.getId <| ←
            `(expand_foldr% ($x $y => $scopedTerm') $init' [$$(.ofElems $id),*])
          boundNames := boundNames.push id.getId
          boundType := boundType.insert id.getId .foldr
          matchers := matchers.push <|
            mkFoldrMatcher id.getId x.getId y.getId scopedTerm init boundNames
        | _ => throwUnsupportedSyntax
    | `(notation3Item| $lit:ident $(prec?)? : (scoped $scopedId:ident => $scopedTerm)) =>
      hasScoped := true
      (syntaxArgs, pattArgs) ← pushMacro syntaxArgs pattArgs <|←
        `(macroArg| $lit:ident:term $(prec?)?)
      matchers := matchers.push <|
        mkScopedMatcher lit.getId scopedId.getId scopedTerm boundNames
      let scopedTerm' ← scopedTerm.replaceM fun s => pure boundValues[s.getId]?
      boundIdents := boundIdents.insert lit.getId lit
      boundValues := boundValues.insert lit.getId <| ←
        `(expand_binders% ($scopedId => $scopedTerm') $$binders:extBinders,
          $(⟨lit.1.mkAntiquotNode `term⟩):term)
      boundNames := boundNames.push lit.getId
    | `(notation3Item| $lit:ident $(prec?)?) =>
      (syntaxArgs, pattArgs) ← pushMacro syntaxArgs pattArgs <|←
        `(macroArg| $lit:ident:term $(prec?)?)
      boundIdents := boundIdents.insert lit.getId lit
      boundValues := boundValues.insert lit.getId <| lit.1.mkAntiquotNode `term
      boundNames := boundNames.push lit.getId
    | _stx => throwUnsupportedSyntax
  if hasScoped && !hasBindersItem then
    throwError "If there is a `scoped` item then there must be a `(...)` item for binders."

  -- 1. The `syntax` command
  let name ← mkNameFromSyntax name? syntaxArgs attrKind
  elabCommand <| ← `(command|
    $[$doc]? $(attrs?)? $attrKind
    syntax $(prec?)? (name := $(Lean.mkIdent name)) $(prio?)? $[$syntaxArgs]* : term)

  -- 2. The `macro_rules`
  let currNamespace : Name ← getCurrNamespace
  -- The `syntax` command puts definitions into the current namespace; we need this
  -- to make the syntax `pat`.
  let fullName := currNamespace ++ name
  trace[notation3] "syntax declaration has name {fullName}"
  let pat : Term := ⟨mkNode fullName pattArgs⟩
  let val' ← val.replaceM fun s => pure boundValues[s.getId]?
  let mut macroDecl ← `(macro_rules | `($pat) => `($val'))
  if isLocalAttrKind attrKind then
    -- For local notation, take section variables into account
    macroDecl ← `(section set_option quotPrecheck.allowSectionVars true $macroDecl end)
  elabCommand macroDecl

  -- 3. Create a delaborator
  if getPrettyPrintOpt pp? then
    matchers := matchers.push <| Mathlib.Notation3.mkExprMatcher val boundNames
    -- The matchers need to run in reverse order, so may as well reverse them here.
    let matchersM? := (matchers.reverse.mapM id).run
    -- We let local notations have access to `variable` declarations
    let matchers? ← if isLocalAttrKind attrKind then
      runTermElabM fun _ => matchersM?
    else
      liftTermElabM matchersM?
    if let some ms := matchers? then
      trace[notation3] "Matcher creation succeeded; assembling delaborator"
      let matcher ← ms.foldrM (fun m t => `($(m.2) >=> $t)) (← `(pure))
      trace[notation3] "matcher:{indentD matcher}"
      let mut result ← `(withHeadRefIfTagAppFns `($pat))
      for (name, id) in boundIdents.toArray do
        match boundType.getD name .normal with
        | .normal => result ← `(MatchState.delabVar s $(quote name) (some e) >>= fun $id => $result)
        | .foldl => result ←
          `(let $id := (MatchState.getFoldArray s $(quote name)).reverse; $result)
        | .foldr => result ←
          `(let $id := MatchState.getFoldArray s $(quote name); $result)
      if hasBindersItem then
        result ← `(`(extBinders| $$(MatchState.getBinders s)*) >>= fun binders => $result)
      let delabKeys : List DelabKey := ms.foldr (·.1 ++ ·) []
      for key in delabKeys do
        trace[notation3] "Creating delaborator for key {repr key}"
        let delabName := name ++ Name.mkSimple s!"delab_{key.key}"
        let bodyCore ← `(getExpr >>= fun e => $matcher MatchState.empty >>= fun s => $result)
        let body ←
          match key with
          | .app _ arity => ``(withOverApp $(quote arity) $bodyCore)
          | _            => pure bodyCore
        elabCommand <| ← `(
          /-- Pretty printer defined by `notation3` command. -/
          def $(Lean.mkIdent delabName) : Delab :=
            whenPPOption getPPNotation <| whenNotPPOption getPPExplicit <| $body
          -- Avoid scope issues by adding attribute afterwards.
          attribute [$attrKind delab $(mkIdent key.key)] $(Lean.mkIdent delabName))
        trace[notation3] "Defined delaborator {currNamespace ++ delabName}"
    else
      logWarning s!"\
        Was not able to generate a pretty printer for this notation. \
        If you do not expect it to be pretty printable, then you can use \
        `notation3 (prettyPrint := false)`. \
        If the notation expansion refers to section variables, be sure to do `local notation3`. \
        Otherwise, you might be able to adjust the notation expansion to make it matchable; \
        pretty printing relies on deriving an expression matcher from the expansion. \
        (Use `set_option trace.notation3 true` to get some debug information.)"

informal_statement: For any propositions $\varphi$ and $\psi$, if $\psi$ is true, then $\varphi \lor \psi$ is also true.
informal_proof:
First, we assume that $\psi$ is true.
Given the definition of disjunction ($\lor$), the statement $\varphi \lor \psi$ is true if at least one of $\varphi$ or $\psi$ is true.
Since we have assumed $\psi$ to be true, it follows that $\varphi \lor \psi$ is true.
Therefore, whenever $\psi$ is true, $\varphi \lor \psi$ is also true.
This completes the proof.

variable {α : Type u}
informal_statement: The inclusion of the EFQ (Ex Falso Quodlibet) rule in a Hilbert-style logical system allows for the derivation of any statement from a contradiction.
informal_proof:
In a Hilbert-style logical system, which consists of a set of axioms and rules of inference, the EFQ (Ex Falso Quodlibet) rule is a powerful principle that states: "From a contradiction, anything follows." Symbolically, this can be represented as:

If we assume a formula of the form \( A \land \neg A \) (a contradiction), then we can derive any arbitrary formula \( B \).

In the context of the IncludeEFQ class, which extends a given Hilbert system H with the EFQ rule, this means that any system which adheres to this principle now has the capability to derive any statement \( B \) from a contradiction \( A \land \neg A \). 

Formally, if \( H \) is a Hilbert system and \( \text{IncludeEFQ}(H) \) is a system obtained by adding the EFQ rule to \( H \), then for any formula \( B \), we have:

\[ \text{If } H \vdash A \land \neg A, \text{ then } \text{IncludeEFQ}(H) \vdash B \]

This extension significantly enhances the logical system's expressive power by making it possible to derive any conclusion from a contradictory set of premises.
